analysis.one_liner: Requires members of Congress and their families to put their stock holdings in blind trusts.
analysis.headline: The bill has 103 cosponsors from both parties but has sat in the House Administration Committee with no vote since its referral in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every member of Congress, plus their spouses and dependent children, to put investments like individual stocks, commodities, and futures into a blind trust — an arrangement where a third party manages the assets and the owner cannot see or direct what is bought and sold. Members could not touch those holdings until 180 days after leaving office. They would have to certify compliance, and those certifications would be posted publicly. The goal is to remove any chance that a lawmaker's personal finances could be swayed by information they get on the job.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who want to know that the people writing tax, trade, and defense laws cannot personally profit from the market-moving effects of those decisions. It benefits voters by removing a structural conflict of interest, and it also benefits members of Congress who do not trade — or who comply willingly — by restoring public trust in the institution. The public loses nothing material: members would still own the assets, just through blind trusts.

how_it_helps.text: It requires Members of Congress, their spouses, and dependent children to place covered investments — stocks, commodities, futures, and comparable synthetic interests — into a qualified blind trust, where someone else controls the holdings so the member cannot know or act on their performance.
Trusts cannot be dissolved or controlled until 180 days after the member leaves office, preventing lawmakers from timing trades around their tenure.
Members must certify compliance to the Clerk of the House or Secretary of the Senate, and those certifications must be posted publicly online, creating a paper trail voters can check.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children who hold individual securities: they would lose control of those holdings for their entire tenure plus 180 days after leaving office, and bear modest trust-administration costs. No one in the general public pays.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their families

drawbacks.text: The bill carves out an exception for any covered investment a spouse or dependent child receives compensation through in their primary occupation, leaving a channel for household financial interests to remain active.

Compliance rests largely on Members certifying to the Clerk of the House or Secretary of the Senate that the trust was established; the bill does not create an independent audit of those certifications, so a determined violator might evade it on paper.

Widely held investment funds and Treasury securities are excluded, so Members keep much of their wealth in marketable assets; that limits the measure's reach, though it also makes the rule administratively workable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — removing the chance that lawmakers trade on information from their official duties — is real and the cost to ordinary people is essentially nil. The main drawbacks are the exemption for occupation-related holdings and the fact that its enforcement depends on certification rather than an independent audit. Its largest weakness is not in the design but in the fate it has met: the bill has gone nowhere despite House support from both parties, so its promised benefit has not been delivered.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Administration Committee in January 2025, and no committee or floor vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 14, 2025 and referred the same day to the Committee on House Administration.
No further action appears in the record: the committee has not held a markup or reported the bill, and no vote has occurred.
Despite 103 cosponsors including 19 House Republicans, bipartisan backing has not moved the bill out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress who hold or trade individual stocks are better off, since the restriction has not moved and the current rules allowing personal trading remain in place.

sides.party_line_note: Support is genuinely bipartisan — 84 of 217 House Democrats and 19 of 223 House Republicans signed on — but the committee with jurisdiction has not acted.

industries.industry: Members of Congress with active personal trading
industries.note: The bill requires lawmakers and their immediate families to hand control of individual stocks, commodities, and futures to a blind trust, ending the practice of personal trading by sitting members. This is the concentrated interest the bill targets.
Setting up qualified blind trusts for hundreds of members and their spouses would generate modest fee income for firms that administer them.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been referred to the House Administration Committee with no markup scheduled. Ethically focused bills like this often stall in committee, but congressional stock-trading restrictions have drawn repeated bipartisan interest and public pressure this decade; if momentum builds, it could reach the floor, though action in both chambers remains unlikely without leadership backing.
